title: Passive and reflexive
intro: This unit turns verbs around. The passive moves the attention from the doer to what is done: *Bu jaý täzeden guruldy* (this building was rebuilt). With no subject at all, the same ending makes rules and general statements: *Bu ýerde çilim çekilmeýär* (no smoking here). The reflexive is for what you do to yourself: *ýuwunmak* (to have a wash), *geýinmek* (to get dressed). And *öz* gives **myself**, **yourself** and **my own**.

blocks.text: The passive is a suffix right after the verb stem, before every other ending: *ýaz-* (write) → *ýazyl-* (be written) → *ýazyldy* (was written). The new stem is a verb like any other, with all the tenses you know: *ýazylýar* (is written), *ýazyldy* (was written), *ýazylar* (will be written), *ýazylmady* (wasn't written), *ýazyldymy?* (was it written?).

Its shape depends on how the stem ends. After a consonant it is `-Yl`, which follows harmony and rounding like any suffix: *ýazyl-*, *beril-*, *gurul-*, *görül-*. After a vowel it is just *-l*: *okal-*, *dokal-*. After *l*, where *-l* can't follow, it becomes `-Yn`: *bilin-*, *gelin-*. And after *l* with a vowel, the *-la*, *-le* verbs, it is *-n*: *arassalan-*, *gürlen-*.

blocks.text: The verbs whose *t* softens before a vowel ([A1 unit 6](a1-u06)) soften before `-Yl` too: *etmek* → *edil-* (be done), *aýtmak* → *aýdyl-* (be said), *gitmek* → *gidil-*. People can be the subject, with the usual person endings:

blocks.title: *saýlanmak* (to be chosen), past: I was chosen…

blocks.text: Usually the passive leaves the doer out; that is its point. If you do name the doer, put it before *tarapyndan* (by): *Bu haly ejäm tarapyndan dokaldy*, this carpet was woven by my mother. In speech, the active with **they** is just as common: *Bu jaýy täzeden gurdular*, they rebuilt this building.

items.en: This building was rebuilt.
The library was built in 1980.
This carpet was woven by hand.
The room was cleaned yesterday.
This picture was drawn by Aýna.
The letter will be sent tomorrow.
The shop opens at nine.

blocks.text: Passive stems make participles too: *ýazylan kitap* (a book that was written), *elde dokalan haly* (a carpet woven by hand), *satylan maşyn* (the car that was sold). They work like the participles of [B1 unit 5](b1-u05).

blocks.title: One suffix for was built
blocks.text: English needs two words, **was built**; Turkmen puts one suffix in the verb: *guruldy*. And where English says **they** or **you** for people in general, Turkmen often prefers the passive: *Bu ýerde pagta ekilýär*, they grow cotton here.

blocks.title: Shorter forms in print
blocks.text: With a few short stems, the vowel of the passive drops out in writing: you will see *gurlan* beside *gurulan* (*täze gurlan jaý*, a newly built house) and *alnyp* beside *alynyp*. This course writes the full forms.

blocks.title: Look at the stem, not the infinitive
blocks.text: Take *-mak*, *-mek* off and look at the last sound: *gel-* ends in *l*, so *gelin-*; *işle-* ends in a vowel after *l*, so *işlen-*; *oka-* ends in a vowel, so *okal-*. Not `arassalal-`, not `gelil-`.

sections.title: One does: the passive with no subject

blocks.text: Turkmen also puts verbs with no object, such as *gelmek, barmak, girmek, gürlemek, ýüzmek*, in the passive, with no subject at all. The sentence then says what people in general do, or may do: rules, customs, directions. English uses **you**, **one**, **people**, or a sign: *Bu ýerde çilim çekilmeýär*, no smoking here (literally: here, cigarettes aren't smoked).

items.en: No smoking here.
How do you get to the museum?
You don't go inside with your shoes on.
Turkmen is spoken here.
No swimming in this lake.
You can also go to Ashgabat by train.
You go up to the third floor by lift.

blocks.text: With *nädip* (how), this is the usual way to ask how something is done or how to get somewhere: *Wokzala nädip barylýar?* (how do you get to the station?), *Bu söz nädip ýazylýar?* (how is this word spelt?). The answer often comes back in the same form: *Awtobus bilen barylýar* (you go by bus).

blocks.title: No person ending
blocks.text: With no subject, the verb stays in the plain third person: *Bu ýerde çilim çekilmeýär*, not `çekilmeýärsiň` or `çekilmeýärler`. And keep the active for a person: *Ol bu ýerde çilim çekmeýär* is **he doesn't smoke here**.

blocks.title: Nädip or nähili?
blocks.text: *Nädip* asks **how, in what way** something is done: *Nädip barylýar?* *Nähili* asks **what is it like**: *Howa nähili?*, *Ýagdaýlaryň nähili?*

The reflexive `-(Y)n` turns an action back on the doer: *ýuwmak* (to wash something) → *ýuwunmak* (to wash yourself, have a wash); *geýmek* (to put on) → *geýinmek* (to get dressed). You met both in [A2 unit 4](a2-u04) as words; this is how they are made. After a vowel it is just *-n*: *taýýarlamak* (to prepare) → *taýýarlanmak* (to get ready), *daramak* (to comb) → *daranmak* (to comb your hair).

rows.en: he or she is getting dressed

blocks.text: Some reflexives have become words with a meaning of their own. *Görünmek* (from *görmek*, to see) is **to be seen, to appear** and **to seem, to look**: *Daglar uzakdan görünýär* (the mountains can be seen from far away), *Sen ýadaw görünýärsiň* (you look tired). *Çekinmek* (from *çekmek*, to pull) is **to hold back, to be shy** ([A1 unit 12](a1-u12)).

items.en: I have a wash in the morning.
The children got dressed and went to school.
We're getting ready for the trip.
She's combing her hair in front of the mirror.
You look tired.

blocks.title: Same shape, two jobs
blocks.text: After a vowel, the reflexive and the passive of a *-la*, *-le* verb look alike: *taýýarlanmak* is both **to get ready** and **to be prepared**. *Biz taýýarlandyk*: we got ready. *Nahar taýýarlandy*: the meal was prepared, since a meal can't get itself ready. The subject tells you which.

blocks.title: Washing your face
blocks.text: *Ýuwunmak* is the whole wash. For one part of you, keep *ýuwmak* and name the part with its possessive: *ýüzümi ýuwdum* (I washed my face), *elleriňi ýuw* (wash your hands).

*Öz* has two jobs. Before a noun that carries a possessive, it means **own**: *öz öýüm* (my own house), *öz maşynyň* (your own car), *öz dilimiz* (our own language). With the possessive endings on itself, it means **self**: *özüm* (myself), *özüň* (yourself), *özi* (himself, herself).
These forms take the case the verb needs, like any possessed noun. The third person has the pronominal *n* before a case, as in *öýüne* ([A1 unit 9](a1-u09)): *özüni*, *özüne*, *özünden*.

blocks.caption: *öz* in the accusative and the dative
head: Self
Accusative
Dative

items.en: I did it myself.
I bought myself a new shirt.
We live in our own house.
Are you driving your own car?
Look at yourself in the mirror!
The child got dressed by himself.

blocks.text: A reflexive verb doesn't need *öz*: *ýuwundym* already says **I washed myself**. Add it to stress who did it, without help: *Çaga özi geýindi*. On its own after the subject, *özüm*, *özi* means **myself**, **himself** in that sense: *Ol özi gelip aýtdy*, she came and said it herself.

blocks.title: öz-özüne, öz-özünden
blocks.text: *Öz* said twice, with a hyphen, means **on one's own**: *Ol öz-özüne gürleýär* (he's talking to himself), *Gapy öz-özünden açyldy* (the door opened by itself).

blocks.title: öz öýüm, not öz öý
blocks.text: Before a noun, *öz* takes no ending; the noun carries the possessive: *öz öýüm*, *öz kitabyň*, not `özüm öý`. And **for myself** is the dative, *özüme*; **myself** as an object is the accusative, *özümi*.

lines.tk: Geçen ýyl. Köne jaý ýykyldy, soň täzeden guruldy.
lines.en: Last year. The old house was pulled down, then it was rebuilt.

lines.tk: Içi örän owadan! Bu halylar elde dokaldymy?
lines.en: It's beautiful inside! Were these carpets woven by hand?

lines.tk: Hawa, Maryda dokaldy. Ejäm olary özi saýlady.
lines.en: Yes, they were woven in Mary. Mum chose them herself.
Do people go in with their shoes on?

lines.tk: Ýok, aýakgaby şu ýerde çykaryň. Ellerimizi aşhanada ýuwup bileris.
lines.en: No, take your shoes off here. We can wash our hands in the kitchen.

lines.tk: Sag boluň. Kaşki meniň öz öýümde hem şeýle haly bolsa!
lines.en: Thank you. If only there were a carpet like that in my own house too!

summary: The passive goes right after the stem: `-Yl` after a consonant (*ýazyldy, guruldy*), *-l* after a vowel (*okaldy*), `-Yn` after *l* (*bilinýär*), *-n* after *l* and a vowel (*arassalandy*).
A passive stem takes every tense and the person endings: *saýlandym*, *ýazylmady*, *ýazylarmy?*; *tarapyndan* names the doer.
With no subject, the passive gives rules and general statements: *Bu ýerde çilim çekilmeýär*; *Muzeýe nädip barylýar?*
The reflexive `-(Y)n` is for what you do to yourself: *ýuwunmak, geýinmek, taýýarlanmak, daranmak*.
*Görünmek* is **to be seen, to appear, to seem**: *Sen ýadaw görünýärsiň*.
*Öz* before a possessed noun means **own** (*öz öýüm*); with the possessive it means **self** (*özüm, özüň, özi*), in any case (*özüme, özüňi, özüne*).
